summary.text: The preceding integer terms give \(a(5)=171\) and \(a(6)=N=(2^{171}+1)/9\), with the modular computation \(N\equiv3\pmod{18}\). Since \(2^{18}\equiv1\pmod{171}\), it follows that \(2^N+1\equiv2^3+1=9\not\equiv0\pmod{171}\), so the division defining \(a(7)\) is not exact.

full_proof.text:
We show that the recurrence already fails to produce an integer at the seventh term.

Let
\[
a(1)=a(2)=1,\qquad a(n)=\frac{2^{a(n-1)}+1}{a(n-2)}.
\]
The first few terms are obtained by direct substitution:
\[
a(3)=\frac{2^1+1}{1}=3,
\]
\[
a(4)=\frac{2^3+1}{1}=9,
\]
and
\[
a(5)=\frac{2^9+1}{3}=\frac{513}{3}=171.
\]
Thus the next term is
\[
a(6)=N:=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}.
\]
This quotient is an integer. Indeed, the stronger congruence established below gives
\(2^{171}\equiv 26\pmod{162}\), and in particular
\(2^{171}\equiv26\equiv-1\pmod 9\). Hence \(9\mid 2^{171}+1\). Explicitly,
\[
N=332572817028187686275682948600327513806149983112761,
\]
although the decimal expansion is not needed for the argument.

We first determine the residue of \(N\) modulo \(18\). For this purpose, it is enough to determine \(2^{171}+1\) modulo \(9\cdot18=162\). We begin modulo \(81\). Since
\[
2^9=512\equiv26\pmod{81},
\]
we obtain
\[
2^{18}\equiv26^2=676\equiv28\pmod{81}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
2^{27}=2^{18}2^9\equiv28\cdot26=728\equiv-1\pmod{81},
\]
because \(728=9\cdot81-1\). Squaring gives
\[
2^{54}\equiv1\pmod{81}.
\]
As \(171=3\cdot54+9\), it follows that
\[
2^{171}=(2^{54})^3 2^9\equiv 1^3\cdot26=26\pmod{81}.
\]
Moreover, both \(2^{171}\) and \(26\) are even. Therefore their difference is divisible by both \(81\) and \(2\). Since \(81\) and \(2\) are coprime, their difference is divisible by \(162\), so
\[
2^{171}\equiv26\pmod{162}.
\]
Hence
\[
2^{171}+1\equiv27\pmod{162}.
\]
Using the exact equality \(9N=2^{171}+1\), this says
\[
9N\equiv27=9\cdot3\pmod{162}.
\]
Equivalently, \(162\mid9(N-3)\). Dividing this divisibility relation by \(9\) yields
\[
18\mid N-3,
\]
and therefore
\[
N\equiv3\pmod{18}.
\]

Now consider the division required to define the seventh term. Since \(a(5)=171\) and \(a(6)=N\), the recurrence would require
\[
a(7)=\frac{2^N+1}{171}.
\]
We compute the numerator modulo \(171\). The elementary identity
\[
2^9=512=3\cdot171-1
\]
shows that
\[
2^9\equiv-1\pmod{171}.
\]
After squaring,
\[
2^{18}\equiv1\pmod{171}.
\]
Because \(N\equiv3\pmod{18}\), there is an integer \(q\ge0\) such that \(N=18q+3\). Thus
\[
2^N=2^{18q+3}=(2^{18})^q2^3\equiv1^q\cdot8=8\pmod{171}.
\]
It follows that
\[
2^N+1\equiv9\pmod{171}.
\]
Since \(9\ne0\pmod{171}\), the integer \(171\) does not divide \(2^N+1\). Therefore
\[
\frac{2^N+1}{171}
\]
is not an integer. In other words, \(a(7)\) is nonintegral even though all the preceding terms through \(a(6)\) are integers. This is a counterexample to the conjecture that every term of the recurrence is an integer.
